entries.title: Online communication with different types of friends and mental well‐being of adolescents in Sweden: A pooled cross‐sectional study
entries.abstract: BACKGROUND: Young people's extensive internet and social media use has raised concerns about potential impacts on their mental well-being. Although many studies have examined general time spent online, fewer have focused on the specific nature of adolescents' online interactions. METHODS: Using a sample of 15-year-olds (N = 3034) participants from the 2017/2018 and 2021/2022 Swedish Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) surveys, we employed pooled cross-sectional linear regression models to examine associations between the frequency of online communication with different types of friends and mental well-being, assessed by the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (SWEMWBS). RESULTS: Online communication was associated with adolescents' mental well-being, but patterns varied by both frequency of communication and the type of friendship. Intense online communication with close friends (b = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.57-2.70) and larger friend groups (b = 1.03, 95% CI: 0.44-1.62) was positively associated with mental well-being. Conversely, communication with virtual friends was associated with poorer well-being (moderate: b = -1.02, 95% CI: -1.50, -0.43; intense: b = -0.61, 95% CI: -1.14, -0.08). These associations remained robust even after model adjustment. CONCLUSION: The findings show that associations between online communication and adolescents' mental well-being differ depending on the type of friend with whom they communicate. These contrasting patterns highlight the need to distinguish between different forms of internet and social media use, and efforts to support young people's online activity should consider not only time spent online but also the nature of their online interactions.

entries.title: Mental Health Effects of Social Media Use Among Adolescents Across Educational Stages: A Meta-Analysis
entries.abstract: Background The link between social media use and adolescent mental health is widely studied, but its variation across developmental stages remains insufficiently clarified. This meta-analysis aimed to compare the differential associations among primary, middle, and high school students. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Embase, and CNKI up to 1 February 2026. Eligible studies reported correlation coefficients between social media use and mental health in school-aged youth. Analyses were performed using Stata 17.0 with random-effects model, subgroup stratification, heterogeneity testing, publication bias assessment, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Results Twelve studies with 15 effect sizes were included. Social media use was significantly associated with worse mental health (r = 0.308, 95%CI: 0.239–0.374, p < 0.001) with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 93.85%). The association differed significantly by stage (Q = 9.72, p = 0.008): strongest in primary school students (r = 0.367), followed by high schoolers (r = 0.334), and weakest in middle schoolers (r = 0.201). No significant publication bias was detected; results were stable. Conclusions The association between social media use and mental health varies significantly across educational stages, with primary school students being the most vulnerable. Developmentally tailored prevention and intervention strategies are needed for school-aged youth.

entries.title: Stressor–Strain–Outcome Dynamics of Digital Distractions: Investigating Social Media Usage, Subjective Well-Being, and Academic Performance Among University Students
entries.venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
entries.abstract: Background: With the rapid development in technologies and social media applications, university life has changed completely when it comes to daily activities and communication as well as the educational settings. Though, on the one hand, platforms like Instagram, Snapchat, YouTube, and WhatsApp bring numerous possibilities for networking, collaborative learning, and sharing educational resources, on the other hand, their frequent use creates serious problems on psychological and academic levels. The present study is going to explore the interdependent relationships between social media usage (SMU) patterns, subjective well-being (SWB), and academic performance of university students at the University of Sargodha in Pakistan. Particularly, the research will analyze such aspects as social media usage frequency, platforms used, reasons for using social media, effects on psychology such as upward social comparisons and related academic results.A descriptive research methodology has been chosen for conducting this research. A sample of 331 students from undergraduate and graduate programs at various faculty of the University of Sargodha was selected using a stratified random sampling method. To collect data, questionnaires were used including measures of social media usage, subjective well-being scales and academic performance indicators. Analyses have been made with the help of statistical software SPSS Version The results show that social media is an integral part of college students' lives and most of them are actively using it daily on a smartphone for more than three hours with a view to socializing, entertainment, and education. However, whereas moderate and goal-directed use is positively correlated with collaboration and academic motivation, compulsive and obsessive use causes serious academic and psychological risks. Constant access to idealized images of peers stimulates social comparison and leads to higher levels of anxiety, stress, and poor psychological well-being. Besides, digital task-switching is not related to learning and long periods of time spent online are linked with cognitive distraction, time substitution, late assignments, and lower grade point average. Social media plays a double role in university students' life since it functions both as an efficient means of education and as a cause of psychological problems and academic challenges. To create a healthy balance between them, the following measures should be taken by institutions and educators.
